content: 1. A study conducted in Murcia in 2019 examined 346 healthy, full-term singleton births. It compared infants breastfed for ≤4 months versus >4 months, assessing their height, weight, and BMI, including rates of overweight and obesity. 2. A prospective cohort study in France in 2019 included 1,028 children who were breastfed or formula-fed for <4 months, 4–<6 months, or ≥6 months. The study evaluated sleep quality and quantity, including sleep onset difficulty, nighttime waking, and sleep trajectory. 3. Another French study in 2021 analyzed 8,696 singleton or twin full-term infants breastfed for <4 months, 4–6 months, or >6 months. It focused on sleep quality and quantity, including sleep duration and nighttime waking. 4. A retrospective cohort study in Egypt in 2016 involved 655 healthy infants aged 6–24 months. It compared those breastfed before 6 months versus after 6 months, examining hemoglobin levels, hematological parameters, and micronutrient status (iron, zinc, copper, and vitamin B12). 5. A 2016 study in Cameroon assessed 212 healthy children aged 5–24 months and 2–5 years. It found that 9% were breastfed during the first 6 months of life. The study measured height/length-for-age z-scores, weight-for-age z-scores, and weight-for-height/length z-scores. 6. A Nigerian study in 2004 included 345 normal birthweight babies less than 14 days old. It compared those breastfed before 4 months versus between 4–6 months, analyzing mean monthly weight gain and morbidity (fever, diarrhea, and acute respiratory infections). 7. A 2017 Brazilian study examined 4,106 healthy adolescents aged 18–19 years who were breastfed from birth. It assessed fat mass index and free fat mass index. 8. A program evaluation in Bangladesh in 2016 studied 2,189, 2,074, 1,969, and 1,885 mother-child dyads at 3, 9, 16, and 24 months of infant age. It compared exclusive breastfeeding for ≤4 months, 5–6 months, and ≥7 months, measuring length-for-age z-scores, weight-for-length z-scores, and stunting. 9. A retrospective cohort study in India in 2002 analyzed 8,977 ever-married women and 6,226 infants breastfed for <6 months, 6 months, or >6 months. It assessed height-for-age and stunting. 10. A 2017 study across Belgium, Cyprus, Estonia, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Spain, and Sweden included 10,808 healthy children breastfed exclusively or in combination with formula for 1–3 months, 4–6 months, or 7–12 months. It measured height, weight, and BMI. 11. A 1977 UK study involved 821 full-term infants breastfed or bottle-fed for <6 weeks, 6 weeks–3 months, or >3 months. It assessed weight gain and linear growth. 12. A 2020 Mexican study included 263 healthy full-term infants breastfed for <4 months or ≥4 months. It measured length, weight, BMI, BMI z-scores, waist circumference, overweight, obesity, and wasting. 13. A 2014 US study analyzed 1,077 participants aged <20 years who were breastfed for <3 months, 3–6 months, 7–11 months, or ≥12 months. It examined the risk of type 1 diabetes. 14. A 2016 Thai study included 41 healthy full-term infants aged 16–20 weeks who were formula-fed for 4–6 months or at 6 months. It assessed weight, length, head circumference, morbidity (respiratory and gastrointestinal infections), and food preferences. 15. A 2015 Indian study analyzed 5,457 children breastfed for <6 months, 6–8 months, or 9–11 months. It measured height, weight, stunting, wasting, and underweight. 16. A 2016 Irish study included 709 healthy maternal-infant dyads breastfed for <17 weeks or >26 weeks. By 6 months, 22% of infants were receiving formula with breastfeeding. It assessed height, weight, waist circumference, atopic dermatitis, and fat mass index. 17. A 2018 Danish study analyzed 77,251 liveborn full-term singleton births with no siblings in the cohort. It compared breastfeeding for <4 months versus ≥4 months, assessing weight, height, and BMI z-scores. 18. A 2008 UK study included 15,980 healthy full-term infants breastfed or formula-fed for ≤1 month, 2–3 months, 4–5 months, or ≥6 months. It examined diarrhea and lower respiratory tract infections. 19. A 2014 US study analyzed 14,200 healthy, normal birthweight children breastfed for <4 months, 4–5 months, or ≥6 months. It assessed overweight and obesity. 20. A 2014 Turkish study included 4,990 healthy children aged 2–14 years breastfed for <4 months, 4–5 months, or ≥6 months. It measured height, weight, and BMI, including rates of overweight and obesity. 21. A 2010 Indian study analyzed 514 healthy, normal birthweight babies, including preterm infants, breastfed for <4 months, 4 months, 5 months, or ≥6 months. It assessed cognitive function. 22. A 2016 Dutch study included 4,919 singleton, liveborn, healthy children breastfed for <4 months, 4–4.9 months, 5–5.9 months, or ≥6 months. It measured bone mineral density, bone mineral content, area-adjusted bone mineral content, and bone area. 23. A 2012 Iranian study analyzed 511 healthy students, including low birthweight infants. It measured height, weight, and BMI, including rates of underweight and overweight. 24. A 2018 Dutch study included 2,611 full-term infants, including low birthweight infants, breastfed or formula-fed for <4 months or ≥4 months. It assessed length, weight, and BMI. 25. A 2017 Chinese study analyzed 18,844 live singleton births breastfed for 3–6 months or ≥6 months. It measured anemia and hemoglobin levels. 26. A 2004 UK study included 604 full-term healthy infants breastfed for <3 months, 3–4 months, or >4 months. It assessed weight gain and morbidity (diarrhea, rash, infections). 27. A 2013 Dutch study analyzed 3,184 healthy full-term children, including low birthweight infants, breastfed for 0–3 months, 3–6 months, or ≥6 months. It measured weight-for-height z-scores and diarrhea. 28. A 2014 Australian study included 242 mothers and infants breastfed for ≤23–56 days or ≥6 months. It assessed height, weight, and BMI. 29. A 2016 German study analyzed 83 healthy full-term newborns breastfed for <6 months or >6 months. It measured height, weight, hemoglobin levels, and hematological details. 30. A 2011 US study included 6,750 children breastfed for ≥6 months, 4–5 months, or ≤3 months. It measured weight-for-length percentiles.
